newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Bank Negara chief warns ringgit speculators - agency.
newsitem.headline: Bank Negara chief warns ringgit speculators - agency.

text.p: Bank Negara Malaysia's Governor Ahmad Mohamed Don on Wednesday warned of stern steps against ringgit speculators, the national Bernama news agency reported.
"Bank Negara will not hesitate to introduce measures to curb such speculative activities." Ahmad told Bernama in an interview.

Ahmad was quoted as saying that the central bank had been in the process of normalising interest rates to levels which had prevailed before its intervention in the foreign exchange market in May following a speculative attack on the Thai baht.
"Now we have no choice but to allow the rates to go up again," he added, stressing that this was warranted by the current situation.
"Otherwise we will only be inviting speculative activity in the ringgit if the rates are not allowed to rise given the shortage of ringgit in the market," he said.

Dealers said Bank Negara was reported to have intervened strongly in the market on Tuesday, spending an estimated $1.0 billion to help the ringgit end the day at 2.5060/70 against the greenback from 2.5247/52 at Monday's close.
Ahmad confirmed intervention by Bank Negara to defend the ringgit, but declined to give the amount of its dollar sales.
Asked about cost and the extent of Bank Negara's intervention in the market, the governor told Bernama: "In pursuing any objective, there is a cost involved."
The intervention was warranted in the interest of long-term stability, he told Bernama. He stressed that the central bank had sufficient reserves to meet such intervention.
Ahmad also confirmed that according to the central bank's monitoring of the market, speculators had been the main sellers of the ringgit since the baht crisis began.

He said the massive and continuous buying of U.S. dollars in the spot and forward markets for non-trade related activies had contributed to destabilising the domestic financial markets. "Such kind of disruptive activities has gone on for too long."
The governor acknowledged that "while we are concerned about the impact of any such measures (to curb speculation), these measures will not affect genuine portfolio and direct investors".
